formationLabel: Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish using the North College Street church from 1920 · closure approved December 2006
currentUse: Holy Cross Parish is closed. Its former church at 18 North College Street survives in commercial use associated with Cohoes Design Glass Associates; a historical directory also preserves the address as 19 North College Street. The Diocese of Albany directs Holy Cross institutional-record inquiries to St. John the Evangelist Church. The official routing proves records custody, not merger or canonical succession.
summary: Holy Cross was Schenectady's Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish. In 1920 the community acquired a former synagogue on North College Street, and surviving church-record surveys begin its registers in 1921. Diocesan closure was approved in December 2006. The former church remains standing in stained-glass business use, while the Diocese of Albany directs parish-record inquiries to St. John the Evangelist. Holy Cross Cemetery at 1456 Dunnsville Road in Rotterdam remains a separate memorial site linked to the Lithuanian community.

historicalNarrative.text: Holy Cross was Schenectady's Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish, distinct from the city's Polish and Polish National Catholic institutions. A state church-record survey places Holy Cross at 18 North College Street from 1920 and dates its surviving registers from 1921. Those dates establish a functioning parish and record series, while the exact erection or incorporation instrument remains unresolved.

historicalNarrative.text: The parish church reused an earlier Jewish worship building rather than beginning with new construction. The Schenectady County Historical Society says a synagogue built on North College Street in 1891 became Holy Cross after 1920 and served a Lithuanian Catholic community. The prior synagogue and later parish are consecutive occupants, not one institution.

historicalNarrative.text: Historical address sources preserve a small but material street-number conflict. The church-record survey uses 18 North College Street, while the Schenectady Digital History Archive directory lists Holy Cross at 19 North College Street. Current local site documentation again uses 18 North College Street. The evidence supports one North College Street church but does not justify silently discarding the alternate number.

historicalNarrative.text: Contemporary reporting says Bishop Howard Hubbard approved Holy Cross's closing in December 2006 after recommendations from the parish council and the diocesan Presbyteral Council. The report distinguishes the approval from Father Richard Carlino's October announcement that closure was likely. The exact decree, effective date, final Mass, and disposition of parish assets were not located.

historicalNarrative.text: The former church building followed a separate life after parish closure. A 2010 historical-society account identified the North College Street structure as a stained-glass manufacturing facility, and current local documentation names Cohoes Design Glass Associates at 18 North College Street. These sources support a standing converted building, not continued Catholic worship.

historicalNarrative.text: Two other continuities remain separate from the building. The Diocese of Albany directs Holy Cross records inquiries to St. John the Evangelist, which establishes records routing but not merger. Lithuania's official 2024 U.S. heritage list identifies Holy Cross Cemetery at 1456 Dunnsville Road in Rotterdam; secondary field documentation associates that cemetery with the Lithuanian parish and reports a 1930 establishment date.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The 1920 value is a North College Street acquisition/use milestone and the 1921 value begins the surveyed register series; neither is treated as a fully proved canonical erection date. Sources alternate between 18 and 19 North College Street for the same church. December 2006 is a reported closure-approval month, while the effective decree date and final Mass remain unresolved.
gaps: The parish's erection or incorporation instrument; any earlier hosted-worship sites; exact blessing and dedication dates; the reason for the 18/19 address discrepancy; the closure decree, effective date, final Mass, and asset disposition; the nature of any institutional continuity beyond records custody; cemetery ownership, governance, record custody, and current burial status; and the former church's interior condition remain unresolved.
